# Power station size for a fridge during an outage

Check three numbers: surge watts, running watts, and watt-hours. Surge is the one that most often decides whether a unit works.

## 1. Surge watts (must start the compressor)
- Plan on **at least 1,300 W of surge**. A larger French-door or older fridge can spike to 1,800-2,400 W ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- A station with plenty of battery but a weak inverter will trip when the compressor kicks on.

## 2. Running watts and waveform
- A full-size fridge runs at roughly 100-250 W, so almost any 1,000 W-class station covers this.
- Choose a **pure sine wave** inverter, which is standard on reputable LiFePO4 units.

## 3. Watt-hours (how long it runs)
- The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so the daily average is low. An ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft model averages about 41 W. Other sources estimate 50-70 W.
- **One day needs about 1,400 Wh** of rated capacity, which includes inverter losses and 20% headroom ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- To size for your own fridge, take the kWh/year on its EnergyGuide label, multiply by 1,000, and divide by 8,760 to get average watts. Then multiply by hours, divide by about 0.85 for inverter losses, and add some margin.

| Outage length | Rated capacity to look for |
|---|---|
| Up to ~12-17 hours | ~1,000 Wh |
| ~24-33 hours | ~1,500-2,000 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800 Wh |
| 3 days | ~4,200 Wh |

HomeGrid HQ's estimates, which assume a 150 W fridge at a 35% duty cycle, put a ~1,070 Wh unit at about 17 hours and a ~2,040 Wh unit at about 33 hours ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). Keeping the door shut stretches these numbers, and warm rooms or frequent opening shorten them.

## Options that fit
- **~2,000 Wh class (about a day and a half):**
  - [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) has 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W output, 3,000 W peak, pure sine wave, and was listed at $699.99 after coupon. Anker's page describes it as built for refrigerator backup.
  - [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l) has 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W output, 3,600 W peak, and LiFePO4 chemistry. It expands up to 8,192 Wh with add-on batteries. It lists at $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF, which Dealectric tested in BLUETTI's cart on 2026-10-21. That link is an affiliate link.
- **~1,000 Wh class (about half a day):** BlackBox Supplies names the BLUETTI AC180 (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W peak) and Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 as options, at roughly $400-800 depending on sales. See their [guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) for current prices and links.

## Bottom line
For most people, a **~2,000 Wh station with at least 1,500 W continuous and 2,700-3,000 W surge** is the safe choice. It covers a typical overnight to 24-hour outage with room for a router and some lights. If outages in your area run longer, pick an expandable model or add solar.

Before buying, check your fridge's manual or label for its startup requirement. Note that some of the surge figures above are allowances based on one example fridge, not guarantees for every model.
